study.title: Lecture 8 on preferences and preference data
study.locator: Lecture 8: On Preferences and Preference Data (Chapters 10 and 11); full lecture video on the course page https://rlhfbook.com/course

focus: On-policy means pairs drawn from the current model family. Different models have different generation patterns, so pooled third-party completions miss the regions the policy will actually visit.
The chosen answer is better relative to the shown alternatives, not globally correct. All compared completions can be correct, or all incorrect, and the pair still teaches.

A Likert integer records a ranking between shown responses, which differs from a rating of one response alone. An even scale such as the 8-point form removes ties, and the result is still binarized for reward training.

Multiturn collection continues from the chosen answer, unrolls every turn into its own prompt, and masks all previous turns from the loss. Structured domains build pairs automatically but the constraint must stay inside the prompt.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write a one-paragraph target-preference definition for a summarization task: feedback types used, prompt sampling, annotator population, rubric axes, and the tie and disagreement policy. State why the pairs must come from the current model family.
traps: Reading chosen as correct. A preference pair orders two outputs; correctness needs a verifier, which arrives in a later unit.
Treating on-policy as the exact current checkpoint. The book uses it softly for the current model family, which is stricter than pooled data but looser than per-update sampling.
Assuming vendor data matches downstream users. Professional labeling settings, interfaces and repetition shift preferences, so audit transfer instead of assuming it.

selfTest.q: Why should preference pairs come from the current model family rather than a pool of popular third-party outputs?
selfTest.a: Each model family has its own generation patterns. Training on pooled outputs teaches distinctions in regions the policy never visits and misses the regions it will visit, so optimization pressure lands in the wrong place.

selfTest.q: What does the 8-point Likert scale remove, and what happens to its labels at training time?
selfTest.a: Its even scale removes the tie option. The labels are still reduced to a binary chosen and rejected signal for reward-model training.

selfTest.q: Can a well-labeled pair teach anything when both completions are factually correct?
selfTest.a: Yes. The label records which response is clearer, safer or more helpful relative to the other, and the reward model learns that ordering.

selfTest.q: How is multiturn preference data turned into training prompts?
selfTest.a: Each turn becomes one prompt that continues from the chosen answer, and every previous turn is masked from the loss so only the judged turn teaches.

units.title: Preference triples, Bradley-Terry likelihood and reward identifiability
outcomes: Derive the Bradley-Terry sigmoid form from exponential strengths and the pairwise negative log-likelihood loss.

units.why: The reward model learns differences, not absolute quality. Misreading its scores as calibrated quality breaks every later claim about margins, scales and KL penalties.

next.note: Implement this loss with a scalar head and measure it on held-out pairs.

study.title: Reward learning lecture with the preference-query reading
study.locator: Lecture 08: Reward Learning on the course timeline https://cs224r.stanford.edu/ (Week 4) with the Christiano et al. preference paper as its listed reading

focus: Preference probability depends only on the score difference. With \(\Delta = r_{\text{c}} - r_{\text{r}}\), the model is \(P(y_c \succ y_r \mid x) = \sigma(\Delta)\) and the per-example loss is \(\mathcal{L} = -\log \sigma(\Delta)\).
Maximum likelihood takes the logarithm before averaging over the dataset. Maximizing expected probability is not the same objective as maximizing expected log-probability.
Adding one constant to every reward leaves every pairwise probability unchanged, but multiplying rewards by a constant sharpens every probability. Identifiability is additive, not multiplicative.

A margin \(m\) demands that the difference clear a threshold, per-prompt grouping stops many-completion prompts from dominating, and the K-wise product over a full ranking collapses to the pairwise form when \(K = 2\).
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the sigmoid form from the exponential ratio, then compute the loss for scores 2.0 versus 0.5 as 0.2014 and for equal scores as 0.6931. Show that adding 10 to both scores changes nothing.
traps: Averaging probabilities instead of log-probabilities. The book derivations keep the log inside the dataset expectation for the maximum-likelihood reason.
Reading a reward of 5 as good in absolute terms. Scores from two runs share no scale, so only differences within one model and data distribution order outputs.
Treating K-wise ranking as a different model family at K equal to 2. The product has one factor left and equals the pairwise probability.

selfTest.q: Show that adding a constant to every reward changes no pairwise probability.
selfTest.a: Each numerator and denominator gains the same factor \(e^c\), which cancels, so only the difference \(\Delta\) enters \(\sigma(\Delta)\).

selfTest.q: What loss does a tied pair produce, and why?
selfTest.a: With \(\Delta = 0\), \(\sigma(0) = 0.5\) and \(-\log 0.5 = 0.6931\). The model is maximally uncertain.

selfTest.q: Why must the logarithm come before the dataset average?
selfTest.a: Maximum likelihood maximizes the expected log-probability of the observed choices. Averaging probabilities first defines a different, incorrect objective.

selfTest.q: A margin of 3 applies to a pair whose reward difference is 1. What is the loss?
selfTest.a: The margin loss is \(-\log \sigma(1 - 3) = -\log \sigma(-2) = 2.1269\). The margin requires the difference to clear 3, so a difference of 1 is penalized heavily.

study.locator: arXiv:2009.01325v3, Sections 1 to 3 (comparison collection, reward training, policy optimization) and the human-evaluation protocol with the length analysis

focus: Read the loss as maximum likelihood over chosen and rejected pairs, as in Maximum likelihood and MAP estimation. The head reads the last non-padding hidden state and one scalar leaves the model per sequence.
Split by prompt, never by pair. Pairs from one prompt scattered across train and held-out sets share prompts and responses, which inflates accuracy.

Report accuracy with the margin distribution and the reward-length correlation. Tiny margins give PPO a weak noisy signal even at acceptable accuracy, and strong length correlation means the data taught longer-is-better.
Fix the reward scale on a calibration set before policy training. Batch statistics drift with the actor, while scores such as 2 versus 1 and 20 versus 10 order identically but drive PPO differently.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, score four fixed pairs with chosen rewards `[2.0, 0.2, 1.0, 0.0]` and rejected rewards `[0.5, 0.1, 1.5, -0.5]`: margins `[1.5, 0.1, -0.5, 0.5]`, accuracy 0.75, mean margin 0.4 and mean loss 0.5735. Then state the split, scale and slice checks that must pass before PPO.
traps: Chasing 100 percent held-out accuracy. Human annotators agree near 80 percent, so typical targets sit at 65 to 75 percent and higher often means overfitting.

Reading large margins as calibration. A large gap can come from overfitting, and ranking accuracy never promises calibrated probabilities; use Calibration curves and Platt or isotonic recalibration and ROC AUC, average precision, log loss and Brier score where probabilities matter.
Training past one or two epochs by default. Preference sets are small relative to backbone size, so validation accuracy usually peaks early and then drops.

selfTest.q: Why must the held-out split separate prompts rather than pairs?
selfTest.a: Pairs from one prompt share the prompt and often share responses. Splitting pairs leaks both sides of the distribution into training, while a prompt split tests generalization to unseen prompts.

selfTest.q: Accuracy is 0.90 but the median margin is 0.05. Should PPO start?
selfTest.a: No. Ordering without separation gives a weak noisy reward signal. Inspect the margin distribution, check for overfitting, and fix the data before optimizing.

selfTest.q: Reward-length correlation is 0.8 on held-out pairs. What caused it and what is the fix?
selfTest.a: Chosen responses are systematically longer, so the model learned longer-is-better. Add rejected long-filler pairs against concise chosen answers and retrain, as the data-flywheel fix describes.

selfTest.q: Two reward models output (2, 1) and (20, 10) on the same pair. Do they agree, and does PPO behave the same?
selfTest.a: They order the pair identically but drive PPO differently: the small scale is drowned by the KL penalty and the large scale dominates it. Normalize on a fixed calibration set first.

study.title: Outcome versus process rewards with hand recomputation
study.locator: Sections 1 to 4: sparse-reward masking, discounted return with \(\gamma = 0.9\), GAE and token-level loss limits, ORM and PRM definitions with aggregation, and the three-condition test for needing process reward (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Recompute the discounted weights by hand. The page prints 0.98 where the arithmetic gives 0.9 to the 8th power, about 0.43; trust your calculation.

focus: An outcome model broadcasts one binary outcome label to every completion token and trains binary cross-entropy there. A process model trains only at step boundaries, such as separator tokens, with correct, neutral and incorrect classes.

With only a final reward of 1 and \(\gamma = 0.9\) over nine steps, early steps get weights down to \(0.9^8 \approx 0.43\). Distance discounting punishes early assumptions even when they determine everything downstream.
Aggregation is a decision, not a default. Outcome scores aggregate by mean, minimum or product, and process scores aggregate over steps by mean, minimum or late-weighted sums.
A pairwise model trained on correct versus incorrect pairs is still a Bradley-Terry contrastive model. An outcome model needs independently labeled sequences without same-prompt pairing.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the per-token outcome loss and the per-step process loss from memory, state which positions carry labels in each, and compute the nine-step discounted weights for a final reward of 1 with discount 0.9.
traps: Reading outcome per-token outputs as step-correctness scores. Every token repeats the outcome label, so reasoning errors that still reach the right answer are reinforced, not flagged.
Treating token-level policy losses as process supervision. Per-token weighting still starts from one terminal signal with no independent judge of each step.
Buying step labels before defining steps. Equation transforms, code edit-compile-test cycles and tool calls are stable boundaries; token counts are not.

selfTest.q: How do outcome models and value functions differ if both emit per-token numbers?
selfTest.a: Outcome models predict the probability of final correctness from fixed offline labels broadcast to every token. Value functions predict remaining return, usually from on-policy rollouts, and serve as baselines in advantages.

selfTest.q: A proof reaches the right conclusion through a wrong step 6. What does outcome-only training reinforce?
selfTest.a: Everything: the correct prefix, the wrong step and the conclusion share one terminal reward, so the error is reinforced alongside the good reasoning.

selfTest.q: When is process reward worth its annotation cost?
selfTest.a: When steps have stable meaning, intermediate errors propagate and waste budget, and the step judge is more reliable than the generator. Short answers with cheap resampling usually fail this test.

selfTest.q: What did the step-by-step paper report on MATH, and under which setup?
selfTest.a: Process supervision beat outcome supervision on MATH problems with 78 percent solved on a representative test subset, using the paper's candidate generation and best-of-n reranking setup with 800,000 released step labels. It is the paper's result on its setup, not a transferable constant.

study.title: Deterministic verifier with hidden adversarial tests
study.locator: Core requirements and Architecture constraints (deterministic verifier, version binding, immutable rollouts); Milestones C and D (verifier tests, loophole injection, proxy-improves-behavior-worsens case)

focus: A usable verifier promises three properties: determinism on identical inputs, correctness against true answer quality, and speed that never bottlenecks training. Correctness is the subtle one.
Completeness accepts correct answers and soundness rejects wrong ones. Report both rates, because a strict parser can be sound yet incomplete and a lenient matcher the reverse.
Parser boundaries decide rewards as much as math does. Boxed-answer extraction, numeric tolerance and symbolic equivalence each accept and reject different equivalent forms.
Verifiers cover only checkable slices. Math, code tests and formal proofs qualify; politeness, creativity and safety do not, and training tests must stay separate from hidden release tests.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write boxed-answer extraction plus grading with string and tolerance comparison, then list four test cases: a correct answer, a wrong answer, a right answer in the wrong format, and an equivalent form such as a fraction versus a decimal.
traps: Counting a missing box as a math failure. Extraction returns no answer and reward 0, which trains format compliance, not reasoning; fix the parser contract or teach format separately.
Equating string equality with answer equivalence. Fractions, decimals, factored and expanded forms need tolerance or symbolic checks, or correct answers fail.
Shipping one verifier as complete evaluation. Visible tests leak into training incentives, so release needs hidden tests the policy never optimized against.

selfTest.q: What do completeness and soundness measure for a verifier?
selfTest.a: Completeness is the rate at which correct answers pass; soundness is the rate at which wrong answers fail. A verifier can be perfect on one and poor on the other.

selfTest.q: The model derives the right number but omits the boxed format and gets 0. Is the math wrong?
selfTest.a: Not necessarily. The parser boundary rejected it before grading. The reward conflates format and math, so either widen the parser or train format as its own objective.

selfTest.q: What separates the minimal classroom verifier from a production math verifier?
selfTest.a: Production adds symbolic equivalence checks, LaTeX parsing and multiple accepted formats where the minimal version uses string matching plus float tolerance.

selfTest.q: What must accompany every verifier score at release?
selfTest.a: Held-out problems plus adversarial and hidden tests with version binding. Training reward is never the sole release metric.

study.title: Data biases that become shortcuts
study.locator: Bias: Things to Watch Out For (verbosity, formatting habits, sycophancy and prefix bias)

focus: Overoptimization differs from overfitting. Overfitting degrades the same task on held-out data; overoptimization improves the proxy while the true goal peaks then falls, so plot quality against KL distance, not just steps.

RL and best-of-n follow different proxy-versus-gold curve forms in the paper setup, and a fixed gold model stands in for humans. Label the curves synthetic overoptimization evidence, never human results.

Length bias is load-bearing evidence, not folklore: the summarization work attributes about a third of the preference gap to length, and the train and test reward split diverges with continued optimization.
Fixes combine data, rubric and constraints. Penalizing length alone treats a symptom; the durable fix feeds bad cases back as rejected pairs, retrains the reward model and holds the KL constraint.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, sketch train-reward rising while gold quality rises then falls against KL distance for RL and best-of-n, then run the flawed length-plus-format reward on one concise and one verbose answer and show the verbose one wins.
traps: Reading the page win-rate table as ties-count-half. Its rows divide wins by wins plus losses, so recompute as wins plus half ties over all outcomes before quoting a rate.

Trusting printed flawed-reward totals exactly. Character-length scoring on the page strings gives larger totals than printed, but both rank the verbose empty answer above the concise accurate one; run the function.
Calling KL penalty a fix by itself. Higher penalties delay overoptimization at a given distance but cost more steps, and ensembles or bigger policies only move the trade-off.

selfTest.q: How does overoptimization differ from overfitting?
selfTest.a: Overfitting memorizes training examples so the same task degrades on held-out data. Overoptimization genuinely improves the proxy while the true goal degrades, because the metric itself diverges from the goal.

selfTest.q: What does the gold-versus-proxy setup establish, and what are its limits?
selfTest.a: A fixed gold model stands in for humans while a proxy trains on its labels; optimizing the proxy traces different curve forms for RL and best-of-n against KL distance. It models human feedback synthetically, so it cannot set human constants.

selfTest.q: Reward correlates 0.8 with length and mean length tripled while reward rose. What is the call?
selfTest.a: Length hacking. Roll back, add concise-chosen versus long-filler-rejected pairs, retrain the reward model, and require the length correlation and manual review to pass before resuming.

selfTest.q: Why is a length penalty alone an incomplete fix?
selfTest.a: It suppresses one exploit without repairing the reward model or the rubric. The policy shifts to the next blind spot such as templates or confident jargon, so pair the penalty with flywheel data and KL control.

A constitution bounds AI feedback but never specifies it exactly. The paper admits principle ambiguity, so every rubric-conditioned run needs human calibration on a sample.
Judge with temperature 0, randomized A and B order with recorded seeds, saved reasoning and a fixed evaluation set. Verdicts without reasoning and seeds cannot be audited later.

Correlated error is the core risk: judge and policy share blind spots, so training on judge labels amplifies them. Anchor the flywheel with an external reward model or human review that the current judge cannot move.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the pairwise judge prompt with order randomization and a JSON verdict, then score five outcomes with 3 wins, 1 tie and 1 loss as 0.7 with ties as half-wins. State the swap test that detects position bias.
traps: Judging with sampling temperature above 0. Rating variance then contaminates every comparison; the book practice fixes temperature at 0 for judge calls.
Treating one strong judge as ground truth. Self-preference and style bias need multi-judge or human audit, and the fixed set must survive judge changes.
Reading a constitution as executable law. Ambiguous principles produce ambiguous labels, so test principle edge cases instead of assuming coverage.

selfTest.q: Why prioritize uncertain comparisons, and what forces recollection?
selfTest.a: Uncertain and disagreement pairs carry the most information per label. The policy distribution shifts under optimization, so yesterday's informative pairs go stale where the policy now samples.

selfTest.q: How do you test a judge for position bias?
selfTest.a: Swap A and B with a fresh recorded seed and rerun. If verdicts follow the position rather than the content, randomize order per prompt and store the seed with every record.

selfTest.q: How do you check self-preference in a judge?
selfTest.a: Compare its verdicts against other judges and against human review on a sampled subset. A judge that favors its own style needs its weight reduced or its rubric rewritten.

selfTest.q: Can AI feedback fully replace human labels?
selfTest.a: No. Scale labeling with AI judges and calibrate direction with humans: spot checks, a fixed evaluation set and an external anchor, so the flywheel cannot merely appease the current judge.

practice.name: Hands-on Modern RL 13.6: order-swapped pairwise judge audit
practice.locator: Run the Preference Evaluation pairwise prompt on a few answer pairs in both orders, compute win rate with `bootstrap_win_rate_ci`, and fill the judge-bias table rows for position, length and self bias (page read 2026-10-14)
practice.note: Runs on CPU. Keep the reasoning, order seeds and human-checked flags with every record.

units.stopWhen: Your judge audit shows position-swap stability, a length-bias readout and a human-checked sample, and you can state which labels the current judge cannot be trusted to produce.

fit.note: The constitutional-AI paper plus the active-learning comparison plus the generative-judge and bias-control sections cover active, AI and biased judging at explain and measure depth.

units.title: Multiple reward components, scalarization and version lineage
outcomes: Implement a multi-component reward with explicit scalarization weights plus length and repetition penalties.
Bind preference, reward and verifier versions to every rollout and evaluation record with an atomic manifest.
State the rollback rule when any component shifts.
units.why: One scalar hides competing goals. Explicit weights plus version binding turn which trade-off shipped into an auditable fact rather than a memory.

next.note: Enforce the manifest and rollback rules at release.
Normalize each component without letting batch statistics drift.

study.title: Hybrid rewards and experiment artifacts
study.locator: The Spectrum of Rewards (hybrid `Rmix` with format, length and correctness weights); Minimal Experiment Directory (data, models and reports layout); quality gates for the data flywheel (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Multi-dimensional fix and bad-case flywheel
study.locator: Multi-dimensional reward fix (`safer_reward` with 0.40 helpfulness, 0.35 correctness, 0.15 format and two 0.05 penalties); The Data Flywheel (bad-case tags such as `length_hack` and `template_hack`) (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Treat the printed weights as one worked choice to implement and vary, not as standard constants.

study.title: Version binding and instrumentation requirements
study.locator: Architecture constraints (every record binds prompt, template, model, reference, reward, verifier and policy versions); Milestone B (instrumentation) and Milestone C (reward and preference implementation)

focus: Scalarization weights are policy, so record them with the run. Helpfulness, correctness and format get positive weights while repetition and excess length get explicit penalties, and length is a penalty term, never a reward.
Normalize each component on a fixed calibration set. Current-batch statistics drift with the actor and hide which component moved.
Group pairwise updates per prompt. Prompts with 9 completions yield 36 pairs against 6 from 4 completions, so ungrouped averaging lets heavy prompts dominate.

A manifest publishes only complete validated artifacts: ordered paths, checksums, counts, versions and RNG state. Failed and filtered rollouts stay counted with explicit reasons, and changed configs reject resume.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write a hybrid reward with separate helpfulness, correctness, format, repetition and length terms plus a manifest listing data, model, tokenizer, template, reward, verifier and policy versions for one run.
traps: Adding a component without versioning it. An unrecorded weight change is an irreproducible experiment, since no later audit can recover the trade-off.
Normalizing rewards on the current batch. The scale then chases the actor distribution and every debug comparison becomes meaningless.
Silently dropping failed rollouts. Deletion changes the estimand, so count failures with reasons in the manifest.

selfTest.q: Why must reward normalization use a fixed calibration set?
selfTest.a: Batch statistics move with the policy, so the same behavior scores differently across steps. A fixed set holds the scale still and exposes which component actually shifted.

selfTest.q: One prompt yields 9 completions and another yields 4. What goes wrong with naive pair averaging?
selfTest.a: The first prompt contributes 36 pairs against 6 from the second and dominates the update. Average pairs within each prompt so each prompt contributes one grouped update.

selfTest.q: What must a run manifest contain to support rollback?
selfTest.a: Data, tokenizer, template, model, reference, reward, verifier and policy versions with ordered paths, checksums, counts and RNG state, covering only complete validated artifacts.

selfTest.q: A format checker ships a bug mid-run. What is the governance call?
selfTest.a: Roll back to the last manifest whose acceptance checks passed, quarantine the affected rollouts, and require the predeclared stop rule before resuming with the fixed checker.

practice.name: Hands-on Modern RL 13.6: scalarized reward with manifest
practice.locator: Implement `safer_reward` on your own answers, vary each weight once, and record a manifest with component versions, checksums and failure counts (page read 2026-10-14)
practice.note: Runs on CPU. Show that a weight change moves the ranking, and that the manifest alone reproduces which trade-off shipped.

units.stopWhen: Your scalarized reward plus manifest reproduces which trade-off shipped, survives a weight change and a checker bug, and rejects resume under a changed config.

fit.note: The hybrid-reward and flywheel sections plus the laboratory version-binding requirements cover scalarization policy and lineage at implement depth.

units.title: Independent evaluation, adversarial tests and reward governance
outcomes: Separate train reward from independent task, human and safety evaluation with a frozen regression set and blinded review.
Build adversarial completions and hidden verifier tests that the policy never trains on.
Write governance rules: ship thresholds, rollback triggers and collection stop rules.
units.why: Training reward always votes for itself. Release needs independent evidence plus written rules for when evidence forces a rollback or stops collection.

next.note: Carry independent evaluation into preference-optimization controls.
Extend adversarial and hacking evaluation to reasoning agents.

study.locator: A Three-Layer Evaluation Stack; Per-Stage Metrics; Training-Time Monitoring checkpoint table; Minimum Acceptance Criteria; Manual Review rubric (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Use the acceptance numbers as course guardrails to implement and tighten, not as industry standards.

study.title: Frozen blinded evaluation with reproduction
study.locator: Milestone F (frozen policies, blinded clean, adversarial and shift evaluation, clean-state reproduction, prespecified extension) and Measurement requirements (paired and seed uncertainty with all attempts preserved)

focus: Answer three questions together, building on Task contracts and automatic metrics: users prefer it, capabilities did not regress, and the reward was not fooled. Benchmarks, preference and manual review each catch what the others miss.
Freeze prompts, decoding and order. Win rates compare only under identical judges, prompts and settings, and small samples need intervals plus manual review of key claims.

Treat contamination probes as bounded evidence, building on Contamination and memorization. Overlap search misses paraphrases and format shifts, and perturbed-variant variance suggests format training without proving contamination.

Write the stop rules before training: ship thresholds, rollback triggers and collection halts. A checkpoint with rising reward, falling regression scores and growing length is a rollback, not a debate.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, read one monitoring row with reward, KL, length, distinct n-grams, regression score and win rate, issue a ship or rollback call with reasons, and write the collection stop rule for length-hack recurrence.
traps: Quoting verifier pass rate as complete evaluation. Verifiers cover checkable slices only; safety, honesty and open-ended quality need independent human and task evidence.
Comparing win rates across different judges or prompts. Rates are comparable only under matched prompts, judges, decoding and item sets.
Reading a clean overlap probe as proof of clean data. Probes miss transformed content while boilerplate triggers false matches, so review matches and bound the claim.

selfTest.q: Which three questions must release evaluation answer at once?
selfTest.a: The model is more aligned with preferences, general and specialized capabilities did not regress, and high-reward responses are truly high quality rather than hacked.

selfTest.q: A checkpoint shows reward 0.45, KL 0.18, mean length 330, distinct-4 0.51, regression 0.70 and win rate 49 percent against SFT. Ship or roll back?
selfTest.a: Roll back. Reward rose while the regression set fell, length grew, diversity collapsed and the win rate sits below half, which matches the suspected-hacking row pattern.

selfTest.q: What are the limits of an n-gram contamination probe?
selfTest.a: It misses paraphrased, translated and reformatted reuse while flagging common boilerplate. High variance on perturbed variants indicates format sensitivity, not proven contamination.

selfTest.q: State a minimal governance bar for an RLHF-versus-SFT comparison.
selfTest.a: Preference win rate above 55 percent with a manual explanation, regression at 95 percent of SFT or better, mean length within 1.3 times SFT, no repetition surge and no safety regression; anything worse rolls back into the flywheel.
